questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Characteristic Equation of a Matrix
questions.problem:
Find the characteristic equation of the matrix 
$B=[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,B-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
B-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}].
$$

Then, the characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-0\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ 5-5\lambda -\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+0 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +5 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix
$M=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by writing the matrix $M-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
M-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & 5 \\ 5 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}].
$$

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $det(M-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & 5 \\ 5 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )-5\cdot 5 & =0 \\ 16+4\lambda +4\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda -9 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-8\pm \sqrt{{8}^{2}+4\cdot 1\cdot 9}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-8\pm \sqrt{100}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-8\pm 10}{2} \\  & =1,-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =1$ and $\lambda =-9.$

$B=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -4 \\ 16 & 12\end{aligned}].$

Let's start by writing the matrix $B-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
B-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & -4 \\ 16 & 12-\lambda \end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & -4 \\ 16 & 12-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )(12-\lambda )-16\cdot (-4) & =0 \\ -48+4\lambda -12\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +16 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix
$P=[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ -5 & 7\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by writing the matrix $P-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
P-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 1 \\ -5 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}].
$$

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $det(P-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(P-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 1 \\ -5 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(7-\lambda )-1\cdot (-5) & =0 \\ 49-7\lambda -7\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+5 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-14\lambda +54 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the discriminant of the quadratic equation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =(-14)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 54 \\  & =196-216 \\  & =-20 \\  & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the characteristic equation does not have real solutions and therefore $P$ does not have real eigenvalues.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Eigenvalues of a Triangular/Diagonal Matrix
questions.problem:
Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix
$N=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{7} & 6 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by writing the matrix $N-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
N-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{7}-\lambda  & 6 \\ 0 & 0-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $det(N-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(N-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{7}-\lambda  & 6 \\ 0 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\sqrt{7}-\lambda )(-\lambda )-0\cdot 6 & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +\sqrt{7}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda =-\sqrt{7}.$

**Note:** The eigenvalues of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix are the entries on the main diagonal.

we see that the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. This is true in general: the eigenvalues of a *triangular* or *diagonal* matrix are *always* given by the entries on the main diagonal!

**Watch out!** For a general matrix (which is neither triangular nor diagonal), this might not be the case!
